entry.title: Tintin or Asterix? Two ways of seeing the world through comic-book genius
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Tintin or Asterix? Two ways of seeing the world through comic-book geniusTintin or Asterix? Two ways of seeing the world through comic-book genius

Tintin makes us curious. Asterix makes us irreverent. Tintin tells us to discover the world. Asterix reminds us not to take its powerful people too seriously

Tintin admirers speak of mystery, adventure, exotic locations, and Herge’s immaculate drawings. Asterix fans counter with puns, satire, Obelix, and the almost therapeutic pleasure of watching Roman soldiers being thrown through the air

Atanu Biswas5 min read Last Updated : Aug 23 2026 | 12:33 PM IST There are questions that should never be answered too quickly. Tea or coffee? Cats or dogs? And, for anyone who grew up with European comics, the most dangerous of all: Tintin or Asterix?   Certainly, they aren’t Tweedledum and Tweedledee. Tintin admirers speak of mystery, adventure, exotic locations, and Herge’s immaculate drawings. Asterix fans counter with puns, satire, Obelix, and the almost therapeutic pleasure of watching Roman soldiers being thrown through the air. The sensible answer is that neither is “better”. They are different kinds of genius.   August 14 marked the birth centenary of Rene Goscinny, the brilliant French writer who, with artist Albert Uderzo, created Asterix. Goscinny possessed the rare gift of making children laugh immediately, and laugh again years later as adults. Perhaps the simplest difference is this: Tintin makes the world larger; Asterix makes the powerful people in it smaller.    The young Belgian reporter travels from Europe to China, Egypt, and Tibet; from South America to imaginary West Asian kingdoms; and even to the Moon. Most journalists write articles. Tintin spends his professional life discovering secret societies, hunting criminals, finding treasure, and getting into situations where gunfire seems part of the job description. His great quality is curiosity.   A Tintin story begins with a puzzle; one clue leads to another until a small mystery becomes a full-scale adventure. In Tintin in Tibet, the adventure becomes something more: A moving story of friendship, loyalty, and determination. In Destination Moon, Herge turns scientific ambition and space exploration into a thrilling adventure, anticipating the fascination that the Moon would inspire in the real world. We turn the page because we want to know what happens next. Herge’s ligne claire, or clear-line style, gives these adventures their visual precision. And then there is the supporting cast: Captain Haddock, Professor Calculus, Thomson and Thompson, and Snowy. Haddock, in particular, gives Tintin’s orderly world a wonderfully human disorder.

   Asterix begins somewhere else entirely. “The year is 50 BC. Gaul is entirely occupied by the Romans. Well, not entirely...” One tiny village refuses to surrender. It has Getafix’s magic potion and an almost supernatural ability to make imperial power look ridiculous. Then there is Obelix, who fell into the potion as a child and, therefore, doesn’t need any more. This may be the most unfair rule in comic-book history: Obelix can throw a Roman regiment around before breakfast. But the Romans are only the beginning of the joke. Goscinny and Uderzo use ancient Gaul to parody the modern world — bureaucracy, consumerism, politics, and the vanity of authority. In Asterix and the Chieftain’s Shield, history becomes a comic battle over food, politics, and dieting; in Asterix and the Roman Agent, propaganda itself becomes a weapon. Caesar may command an empire. He still cannot quite conquer one stubborn village. That’s the joke. It’s also a philosophy.   One travels. The other stays home. Tintin is always going somewhere. Asterix, although he travels occasionally, is remarkably happy to stay where he is. Tintin gives us the world. Asterix gives us a village. And what a village it is: Asterix, Obelix, Getafix, Vitalstatistix, Dogmatix, the fishmonger, the blacksmith, and the unfortunate bard. Tintin’s stories are essentially adventures of an individual; Asterix belongs to a community. Tintin is a journey. Asterix is a neighbourhood.   Perhaps that’s why the village feels so familiar when we return to it as adults. We recognise the argumentative neighbour, the pompous leader, the person who always has an opinion — and the person who believes he is perfectly reasonable while everyone else is clearly insane. In other words, we recognise ourselves.   If Tintin’s great strength is plotting, Asterix’s is language. Goscinny was a master of puns, names, and double meanings — a translator’s nightmare. At ten, Captain Haddock is simply funny. Later, we see the mixture of courage, helplessness, dignity, and absurdity beneath the shouting. At ten, Obelix’s Roman-bashing is hilarious. Later, we notice the larger joke: An empire becomes powerless when ordinary people refuse to be impressed by it. The books don’t change. We do.   The difference reflects their creators. Tintin was overwhelmingly the achievement of one artistic imagination: Hergé. Asterix was a remarkable partnership — Goscinny supplied the scripts, jokes, and satire; Uderzo supplied the expressive bodies and kinetic energy. One might put it this way: Goscinny wrote the laughter. Uderzo gave it a structure.   So, Tintin or Asterix? Perhaps the answer is simply both — but not for the same reason. Tintin makes us curious. Asterix makes us irreverent. Tintin tells us to discover the world. Asterix reminds us not to take its powerful people too seriously. A childhood with Tintin gives you wanderlust. A childhood with Asterix gives you a healthy suspicion of emperors. And a century after Goscinny’s birth, that seems like a rather good education.

entry.title: Munir, power, and paranoia
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Munir, power, and paranoiaMunir, power, and paranoia

At some point, Pakistani dictators begin to show paranoia. That's the strategic reality most relevant to India since the late '50s. Munir's case is worse, like some sudden acrophobia

(Photo: Twitter/@asim_mz)

Shekhar Gupta7 min read Last Updated : Aug 22 2026 | 9:30 AM IST The reason all dictators live in paranoia is that they can never have a retirement plan. Today, they might decide the fate of all their subjects, but if they lose power, they can’t determine what happens to them.  That’s why, at some point, Pakistani dictators begin to show signs of paranoia. It’s been the strategic reality most relevant to India since the late 50s, after Ayub Khan took over and promoted himself to field marshal.  Usually it takes about five to seven years for these fears to start oozing out. With Asim Munir, it’s been coming at T-20 speed. This is the era of 30-second Insta reels after all. Since Op Sindoor, he has had at least four phases of bestowing additional powers or ranks upon himself. For now, let’s focus on the latest, this Thursday.   The sudden passage of the two most significant military-related laws in Pakistan National Assembly last Thursday was so dramatic that it would stun the closest watchers of that establishment. It adds even more power, if it was still possible, to what Munir already has.   The Pakistan Cabinet met Thursday morning, approved Defence Forces Act, 2026, and the amended National Command Authority Act, 2010, took them straight to the National Assembly, passed them within 30 minutes and adjourned the house. The Opposition walked out, Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), the second-largest member of the ruling coalition, protested, but voted for the laws anyway. And the President, from the PPP, signed it in a jiffy too. Nobody makes Asim Munir wait. 

Also Read

Pakistan army chief says Balochistan militants are foreign proxies

 Some Pakistani analysts would say these laws only formalise, retrospectively from November 27, 2025, the arrangements resulting from the 27th Amendment, which mutilated the Constitution, created the post of Chief of Defence Forces (CDF), laid down that only the Army Chief could have that position.  It gave Munir a fresh five-year tenure until November 30, 2030, made his field marshal’s rank for life with full benefits, and granted him immunity from prosecution forever. The “it’s nothing new” school would say a retrospective legal framework was needed to formalise the earlier constitutional amendment. On a close reading, however, additional powers Munir has grabbed are formidable. These could only come from a place of deep insecurity, or more likely paranoia. All dictators start fearing their shadow at some point. For Munir, it’s come the earliest.  Under the new laws, it says, Munir can “hire, fire and retire” armed forces personnel. Or extend their tenure at his fancy. This applies not just to some loyal subedar-major or colonel, but to all his peers as well.  Read between the lines, it means he can retire any of his generals, especially Corps commanders, or give them a longer tenure. The first will make them fear him, and the second will make them greedy. There have been signs and whispers of restlessness among Corps commanders, the senior brass chafing at the glass ceiling, with Munir perched atop it, and the entire line of succession blocked. This new law will scare some, give hope to others. A better name for the law could be Pakistan Defence (Formalisation of Sycophancy) Act. The same law, by the way, gives Munir’s latest appointee and loyalist, Syed Aamer Raza, whom he just promoted to four-star general and commander of the newly created National Strategic Command, an indefinite tenure at his field marshal’s pleasure.  How insecure do you have to be to keep finding newer ways, laws, ranks, awards, affirmation of your own position every few months? It’s the oldest truism that all dictators are lonely and scared. In Munir’s case, the better definition of his fears would be acrophobia. He’s risen too high, too soon, has no idea where he’s headed, and is deeply conscious of enemies he has made.  In India, we fret over his “successes” with Donald Trump and in West Asia. The cruel fact, however, is that such stature must rest on the bedrock of comprehensive national power (CNP). That, in Pakistan’s case, is declining. It’s unidimensional, based on its efficient military. The economy is dead and there seems to be no effort to lift it; except to count on the possibility of a largesse from the Saudis. But the Saudis, under debt now, can’t spare more than a couple of billions — if even that — as gratuities to Pakistan for its army’s services. In any case, hope isn’t a plan.  Pakistan’s military also has severe limitations. They can’t close the issue with various rebellions along its western borders or make any military gains against India. They can be no more than a nuisance occasionally. Where does that leave Munir? His genius lies not in military craft but in understanding the vicious praetorian politics of his military-owned state. He also understands the risks. This is by no means normal politics. I can give you a choice of three to describe this: Cutthroat, stab-in-the-back, or take-no-prisoners. Munir can’t insure his future. He has to be obsessed with preserving his present. These new laws, therefore, are a coat of additional armour. That won’t save anybody with a box of mangoes on the plane.  Munir was born in 1968. That makes him young at 58, to be close to the fifth year as army chief, now exalted to Chief of Defence Forces (CDF). On November 30, 2030, when his latest five-year term ends — if it does end — he will be only 62. That’s the age at which an Indian Army chief retires. General Dhiraj Seth is already Munir’s third Indian counterpart and by November 2030, he will have a fifth. Where will he go from 2030, is his challenge.  Many Pakistanis believe he would declare himself president much before that. And it will be a presidency without any tenure. So he can rule forever. They're probably right. But, as the record of his predecessors tells him, time doesn’t stand still.  Ayub and Yahya Khan plotted their decline and humiliation more systematically, through politico-military misadventures in 1965 and 1971, respectively. Zia was consumed by fate at the peak of his power. Musharraf tried to become a Pakistani Ataturk but didn’t have the intellect or peer support. He ended up a convict with a death sentence for treason. Why would the future treat Munir any differently? This is how India must read his mind, his phobic loneliness at the top.  As I have written often, there’s one of three ways a Pakistani dictator goes: Jail, exile or assassination. Musharraf had once “admonished” me for keeping on predicting this fate for him. In Davos, he wagged his finger and said, there was a time we respected your reading of Pakistan, but not now. And he referred to my three-exit theory for dictators. You are wrong, he said, because you think I am a dictator. I am not, I am a democrat.  Dictatorship and delusion go together. But, if I were to do some future-gazing for Munir, I’d see three options, and retiring to go home and play golf isn’t one. He can finish up and quietly go away to America. He’d have his stash and an estate there, and the grateful Americans won’t extradite him even after his successor repeals his immunity. Next, he can pronounce himself president for life like some Robert Mugabe. Or third, that he really turns Pakistan’s economy around, calms down its society, ends internecine conflicts and creates a new Republic. That will inevitably need peace with India, an end to the Kashmir fixation, and the de-Islamising of his nationalism. This will be the safest. It will also be the toughest if not impossible.

Today's opinions examine the Saudi-Turkiye-Pakistan defence pact, leadership challenges at the Tata group, Asim Munir's growing powers and the political potency of negative branding

premium

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Aug 22 2026 | 6:15 AM IST Hello, and welcome to the Best of BS Opinion, our wrap of the day's Opinion page.    Shyam Saran argues that the Saudi Arabia-Turkiye-Pakistan defence pact marks a significant shift in West Asia’s security architecture, driven by declining confidence in US security guarantees, shared concerns over regional threats and closer Saudi-Turkish ties. While the pact promises collective deterrence, differing threat perceptions make a NATO-style defence arrangement unlikely. Saran sees Pakistan’s role as a trusted bridge between Saudi Arabia and Turkiye as particularly significant, enhancing its regional profile and potentially benefiting China. For India, the emerging alignment poses risks to energy security, the safety of millions of Indians in the Gulf and its strategic freedom in responding to cross-border terrorism.   The Tata group’s recent leadership transition raises questions about succession, capital allocation and the development of leaders capable of navigating multiple industries, but not necessarily about its underlying purpose. Its long-standing commitment to serving the nation through enterprise remains evident in investments spanning electric vehicles, batteries, defence and semiconductors, alongside continued philanthropy, writes R Gopalakrishnan. The group’s distinctive structure, with a private holding company and publicly listed operating companies, allows businesses to retain domain expertise while preserving a common institutional ethos. The more pressing challenges are strengthening capital allocation and developing leaders with the breadth and long-term perspective required to guide the group.   Shekhar Gupta suggests that the rapid expansion of Asim Munir’s powers reflects not strength but deep insecurity and paranoia. New laws formalising his authority as Pakistan’s Chief of Defence Forces allow him extensive control over military appointments and tenures, further concentrating power while potentially unsettling the senior brass. However, Gupta points out that Munir’s apparent diplomatic successes cannot compensate for Pakistan’s declining comprehensive national power, weak economy and limited military options. With his current tenure potentially ending in 2030, the fundamental question is what happens to him thereafter. Drawing on the fates of Pakistan’s previous dictators, Gupta sees three possible exits: exile, permanent rule or, most improbably, reforming Pakistan through economic recovery, internal reconciliation and peace with India.   Negative branding has become a powerful political weapon, allowing rivals to be discredited through nicknames, memes, ridicule, fake news and other forms of mockery. Unlike corporate marketing, where attacking competitors can damage an entire market, political branding operates within a zero-sum contest for power and resources. Some of the most effective campaigns, however, writes Devanghsu Datta, have been spontaneous rather than orchestrated, as illustrated by Simon and Garfunkel’s unintended association with Malawi’s political establishment and the Winnie-the-Pooh memes targeting China’s leader. With social media accelerating the spread of such imagery, the ability to turn politicians into objects of ridicule could pose an existential challenge to political leaders' credibility and electoral prospects.     Topics : Saudi Arabia Pakistan Turkey West Asia israel Iran Tata group Tata Sons Tata Trusts India Inc succession planning N Chandrasekaran Cyrus Mistry Ratan Tata noel tata Branding Political satire Winnie the Pooh

entry.title: Statesmen versus CEO: Institutions above individuals
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Statesmen versus CEO: Institutions above individualsStatesmen versus CEO: Institutions above individuals

Corporate leaders' half-life has shrunk over the past few decades. That is the Tata experience as well

premium

Image for Representation

R Gopalakrishnan5 min read Last Updated : Aug 21 2026 | 11:20 PM IST The avalanche of comments about the Tata group has been mind-boggling and I regret contributing to this through this article! A difference of opinion between leaders could not be resolved through discussion, and a planned separation has speedily ended the differences. I note, admittedly through the rear-view mirror, that the institution has been placed above individuals. That is a good thing.  On August 12, the chairman of Tata Sons wrote that he would not offer himself for reappointment in February next year. What would happen next? Rabindranath Tagore had written: “Who will take over my responsibility asked the evening sun, The world was silent upon hearing this question, A tiny mud wick lamp then spoke and said, To whatever extent I am capable, I will light up the world.” (Ke loibe mor karjo kohe sandhyar ravi, Shuniya jagat rohe niruttar chobi, Matir pradeep chilo, shey kohilo swami, aamar jettukko shadyo, koribo ta aami).  Remember how Indians thought of Lal Bahadur Shastri when he succeeded Jawaharlal Nehru? Likewise, when Ratan Tata succeeded JRD Tata; and when Cyrus Mistry donned the mantle of leadership from Ratan Tata in 2012.  If, however, a successor is not announced simultaneously with the exit of the incumbent, then the focus shifts to the circumstance of the exit. Any professional chief executive officer (CEO) serves with support from the board, and lack of clarity may well imply that his or her service may have played out its role.  Corporate leaders’ half-life has shrunk over the past few decades. That is the Tata experience as well. Over 144 years till 2012, Tata Sons had just five chairmen. However, in the 15 years till 2027, the same group will see three. This fact should be viewed as part of more rapid changes in the leadership environment.  I feel that the purushartha of Tata (its purpose) has been pretty much maintained for over a century and a half: To serve the nation and society through enterprise. I respectfully disagree with the view that Tata needs to reassess what it stands for (Business Standard, August 20). Investment in, for example, electric vehicles, batteries, defence, and chips do prioritise national needs. Air India faced an unprecedented bunching last year of high prices of aviation turbine fuel, no-fly over regions, and the unfortunate Ahmedabad accident. The foray into smartphones and semiconductors would have pacified the atma of the late FC Kohli, who bemoaned that India (and Tata) had missed the microelectronics revolution. And all this without affecting the expenditure on philanthropy!  The recent developments do provoke some questions, but not regarding purpose. Here are three.  First question: Has Tata “gotten away” with engaging in multiple businesses?  It is argued that one chairman cannot understand so many domains. However, domain knowledge resides in the operating company. Managers in Tata Consultancy Services or Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles think of nothing but software or mobility. They suffer no distractions. Tata Sons’ representatives on their boards play their fiduciary roles as directors. Tata Sons/Trusts thus acts as a “spiritual” holding company with a fiduciary role (Business Standard, June 27, 2026).  Tata is a unique loose-tight structure, in which the operating companies are public, and the holding company is private. The operating company’s board (which the Tata Sons chairman may or may not be part of) provides the perspectives required for the business. This distinctive structure allows the maximum domain flexibility for its operating companies.  The Tata mandate for its companies is to adopt some things: First, a brand equity and brand promotion agreement to uphold the Tata way; second, a company and personal code of conduct; third, a commitment to excellence through the Tata brand excellence model; fourth, accountability for decent and competitive returns from the business over the long term.  Unlike most global companies, Tata Sons is not listed. It owns shareholding in its 26 listed companies as also in several unlisted companies, apart from supporting investment in new ventures like semiconductors. Recent media reports applaud how GE and Honeywell have “unlocked” value by spinning off their businesses. In that sense, Tata is permanently in a “spunoff state”, and value stands permanently unlocked.  This is one reason why many feel that the “secret sauce” of having the holding company private plus operating company public should not be lost. Listing Tata Sons will be damaging to the ethos and long-term perspective of the group. Further, there is a commercial reason for not listing, which is the holding company discount.  Which sensible enterprise would accept a loss of philosophical moorings and the application of holding-company discounts to satisfy a regulation or for reasons of visibility?  Second question: Does Tata need a tighter capital allocation system?  This question implies that Tata Sons has a method, but the method could do with sharper analysis and execution. This is a fair suggestion. What has worked well in the past can surely be improved for the future.  Third question: Does Tata Sons have a method of producing multispectrum statesmen?  The group chairman must fit culturally, be operationally savvy, but also demonstrate multispectrum statesmanship (MSS). MSS shapes the future of industry, society, and the nation while building successful enterprises. MSS differs from CEOs through scope, the time horizon, and responsibility.  This requirement demands a methodology to develop statesmen through multiple domains. Hence, leaders in Tata Sons need a distinctive capability. Does Tata Sons programme this?   In short, there is a good chance that the stability and organisational capabilities of Tata will produce the immediate results. In the longer term, improved capital allocation and future-ready, statesmen-leader development are issues for the firm.

Ind AS 117, Insurance Sector, Life Insurance, IFRS 17, HDFC Life

insurance

Vibha Padalkar4 min read Last Updated : Aug 21 2026 | 11:17 PM IST Since the opening of the insurance sector in 2000, the industry has witnessed changes at various intervals. Be it products, distribution, servicing – every aspect has undergone changes over the last several years. Among the more recent ones, from the financial point of view is the implementation of the IndAS 117.   The need   For a long time, the insurance sector has perhaps been one of the few industries in India with a need to conform to two reporting frameworks. While the accounting framework that governs financial statements provides a statutory and prudent view, it may not provide an accurate picture of the business profits and financial performance of an insurer. The actual economic or actuarial ‘Embedded Value’ framework captures an insurance business’ economic value more appropriately. It is a known fact that India’s insurers have struggled to cater to two diverse sets of accounting frameworks leading to inconsistencies in assessing a company’s financial health accurately.   Now, with the impending implementation of IndAS 117, the Indian insurance industry stands at the cusp of a transformation in financial reporting. Consistent with the International Financial Reporting Standard (IFRS) 17, the IndAS 117 will fundamentally alter the way in which insurers report profits, liabilities and consequently, record and measure financial performance.   One framework, many benefits   While the ‘Embedded Value’ reporting framework appropriately encapsulates the value of the business on the books, it has a few limitations. Despite its robustness, it is undeniably complex. Consequently, its understanding is limited to industry experts and the industry’s long-term observers. Laypersons find it challenging to draw insights from the framework. Secondly, the ‘Embedded Value’ disclosures exist outside the primary audited financial statements. Accordingly, despite internal and external reviews, it may not receive the same level of audit scrutiny and regulatory oversight as the statutory accounts. And finally, while these disclosures are required to be published by listed insurers, there is no such mandate for unlisted insurers, often leading to an uneven playing field when analysing accounting information. Simply put, it may not facilitate an apple-to-apple comparison between two entities.   The IndAS 117 framework offers an opportunity to insurers to ascertain profits accurately while inspiring the layperson’s confidence in the company’s financial health. Insurers will now be able to represent economic profits in their statutory financial statements in a manner consistent with business intricacies. There are multiple benefits here. It will lend transparency and uniformity to the books of accounts while allowing independent observers to better understand the business. Also, since the accounting standard mandates higher level of disclosures, insurers can better present their economic position. Lastly, aligning with an internationally accepted standard will allow comparison of an Indian insurer’s business strength with a global player, leading to consistent evaluations. It is pertinent considering that the Central Government has now allowed 100% Foreign Direct Investment in India’s insurance sector.   A gamechanger for life insurance business   IndAS 117 will have a more transformative impact on the life insurance business. With life insurance dealing in long-term contracts, the point at which profits for a policy are booked has remained a bone of contention for long. The new standards recognise the concept of Contractual Service Margin (CSM) that is the expected profit locked in a policy and will be released into the books gradually over the policy’s tenure. The CSM may become a key metric for business observers to gauge a life insurer’s long-term business efficiency.   Teething issues   Insurers will need to invest substantially in overhauling current reporting systems as well as enhancing data pipelines to support the new standard’s granularity. Equally important will be training of the concerned personnel. The members of the finance, actuarial, risk, data and technology functions will have to be oriented towards working in close alignment with the on-ground teams.   While operational complexities may pose a challenge, the long-term strategic benefits outweigh the efforts and costs involved. Initially, the new standards may co-exist with the Embedded Value framework as the analyst and investor community relies on the latter for decision-making. Going forward, internationally consistent and enhanced IndAS 117 disclosures should lead to greater comparability, both within the industry as well as with global peers. It will help in attracting larger pools of long-term domestic and international capital giving a fillip to growth and insurance penetration.   Conclusion   Regardless of the initial hiccups, the adoption of the IndAS 117 standard is a pivotal opportunity to align India’s insurers with contemporary accounting conventions.    ________________   The author is managing director & CEO of HDFC Life   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer.
